1.caption: Yin Xi, the keeper of the pass, reads the book Laozi left behind. Notice that he holds the text, but the author is gone.
1.look: Begin with the open scroll in Yin Xi's hands, then let your eye move out to everything that is not the book: the willow, the incense smoke you cannot see, the white page around him. The printer used only black lines, and most of the paper stays empty. This is the first scene in the life of the Daodejing: a reader alone with words that point beyond themselves. The opening chapter warns that the Way which can be spoken is not the constant Way. Yin Xi seems to know this. He reads slowly, as if listening for what the words cannot hold.

1.caption: Mi Youren's hills are only half there; mist takes away their edges. Look for the place where ink stops and nothing begins.
1.look: Mi Youren built these mountains from soft, wet dots laid side by side, so that no line ever closes a shape. Find one hilltop and try to say where it ends. You cannot. The trees dissolve in the same way. The painting lives in the passage between named things and the unnamed mist that holds them. Chapter 1 calls this the gate of all mysteries: being and non-being come out together and differ only in name. Let your eye rest in the grey spaces. They are not gaps in the picture. They are the picture's source.

2.caption: Lu Zhi paints Zhuangzi asleep on a rock while two butterflies drift above him. Which one is dreaming?
2.look: The sleeper lies flat and heavy on the rock; the butterflies are almost nothing, two flicks of the brush in the air. Heavy and light, solid and empty, waking and dreaming: the painting is built on pairs, like this chapter. Laozi says that beautiful and ugly, long and short, high and low give rise to each other. Notice how the willow strands hang down toward the sleeper while the butterflies rise. Nothing here wins. Each thing is itself only because the other is there. Stay with the empty air between the man and the insects.

2.caption: Sengai's square, triangle and circle lean on each other. Each shape is clear only because the others are next to it.
2.look: Read the shapes from left to right, then from right to left. The square is firm and closed; the triangle points; the circle opens. They overlap, so that one stroke belongs to two shapes at once. Sengai never explained the picture, and that is part of its humour. Chapter 2 says that the sage teaches without words and lets things arise without claiming them. The brush here does the same. Look at the dry, broken edges of the ink: the shapes are not perfect, and they do not try to be.

3.caption: Xia Gui puts a few trees and tiny figures on a low bank and leaves the rest as mist. Nothing here asks for attention.
3.look: Look first at the left edge, where the trees and the little figures sit. Then let your eye travel right across the wide, golden emptiness. There is no palace, no treasure, nothing to compete for. Chapter 3 advises not to praise the clever or prize rare goods, so that people are not stirred to quarrel or steal. The sage empties hearts and fills bellies. This painting feels like that kind of life: modest, settled, with plenty of room to breathe. The mist is not a lack. It is the quiet in which the small scene can rest.

4.caption: The gu is a wine vessel whose use is its hollow. Its mouth flares wide, and its centre is mostly air.
4.look: Follow the outline from the wide mouth down to the narrow waist and out again to the base. The bronze is only a thin skin around an empty column. Three thousand years ago this cup held offerings for ancestors. Chapter 4 says the Way is empty, yet using it never fills it up; it is deep, like the ancestor of the ten thousand things. Imagine looking down into the gu from above: a dark round hole with no bottom you can see. The shape is useful because it holds back from being solid.

5.caption: Xia Gui leaves most of the paper blank. The empty space works like the bellows in this chapter: it gives, and it is never used up.
5.look: Look at how much is not painted. Cliffs and pines crowd one side, and everything else is mist and water. Yet the blank paper does not feel weak; it gives the rocks their weight and the trees their reach. Chapter 5 says heaven and earth are like a bellows: empty but not exhausted; the more it moves, the more comes out. Breathe slowly while you look. Let the empty part of the picture breathe with you. The painting does not favour any one thing. Rock, tree and fog are all simply allowed.

6.caption: Hongren's valley is pale and still, with a thin stream running down its centre. The valley spirit does not die.
6.look: Start at the top among the angular rocks and follow the stream downward. The forms are drawn in thin, dry lines with almost no shading, so the whole valley feels open and clean. Chapter 6 speaks of the valley spirit and the mysterious female, the root of heaven and earth, which goes on and on and is never used up. A valley is a low, receiving place. Everything flows into it. Notice that the painting has no strong focus; your eye keeps sinking toward the low, quiet centre, as water does.

6.caption: Kuncan hides a monk's house deep in the folds of the mountain. Find it, and notice how much the valley protects it.
6.look: This painting is crowded where Hongren's is bare. Rock, trees and mist press in from all sides. Take your time to find the small dwelling tucked into the hollow. Once you see it, the whole mountain seems to curve around it like a cupped hand. The valley in Chapter 6 is not empty for its own sake. It gives shelter and gives birth. Kuncan was a Buddhist monk who lived in mountain temples; he knew what it is to be held by a landscape. Let your eye rest in the hollow.

7.caption: The great peak behind the temple has stood for ages. It lasts because it does not live for itself.
7.look: The composition is built on a strong central axis: the mountain at the top, the pagoda below it, the inns and travellers at the bottom. Everything is arranged in layers that rise slowly. Yet the peak does nothing. It gives shade, holds water, shelters the temple, and asks for nothing. Chapter 7 says heaven and earth endure because they do not live for themselves; the sage puts himself last and so finds himself first. Notice how the temple stands lower than the peak and the travellers lower still, and how calm this order feels.

8.caption: Ma Yuan's waves fill the whole leaf with a soft, even net. Water benefits all things and does not compete.
8.look: Look closely at a single wave: one curling line that rises, folds over, and passes its motion to the next. No wave is larger or more important than its neighbours. Then step back and see the whole Yangzi spread out flat and wide. Chapter 8 says the highest good is like water. It nourishes everything, does not contend, and settles in low places that people dislike. Ma Yuan has painted nothing but water, yet the page feels alive. Let your breathing follow the rhythm of the lines.

9.caption: The Daoist Ge Hong moves his family into the mountains, leaving office behind. When the work is done, step back.
9.look: Find the tiny figures crossing the bridge at the lower left: Ge Hong with his household and an ox. Then follow the path upward into the folds of green and blue mountain, where the house waits. Wang Meng crowds the scroll with texture and colour, but the story at its heart is a quiet withdrawal. Chapter 9 warns that filling a hall with gold and jade means you cannot guard it, and that pride in wealth invites disaster. Withdraw when the work is done: that is the Way of heaven. The travellers do not look back.

10.caption: A Han bronze mirror: its polished face is gone, but its back shows the cosmos. Can you clean the dark mirror so that no stain remains?
10.look: This is the back of the mirror. The other side was once polished bronze. Start at the central knob, then circle outward past the seated deities, the chariot and the tiger, to the plain rim. Everything turns around a still centre. Chapter 10 asks a series of questions: can you embrace the One without letting go, soften your breath like an infant, polish the dark mirror until it has no flaw? The mirror was an image for the mind in early China. It reflects everything and keeps nothing.

10.caption: Two small children reach toward a flower. Can you soften your breath and become like a child?
10.look: Watch the children's hands. One reaches forward, the other rests on the ground. They are completely absorbed and do not know they are being looked at. Su Hanchen was famous for paintings of children at play, and he caught their round bodies and quick attention exactly. Chapter 10 asks whether you can concentrate your breath until it is as soft as an infant's. The children here do not try to be soft. They simply are. Their whole being goes into looking at one flower.

11.caption: A Han model chariot: thirty spokes share one hub, and the wheel turns because the hub is empty.
11.look: Look at the wheels. The spokes run inward to the hub, and the axle passes through the hole at its centre. Without that hole there would be no wheel, only a heavy disc. Chapter 11 uses three images: the empty hub of a cart, the hollow of a clay pot, the open space of a door and window. What is there gives benefit; what is not there gives use. This little bronze cart was buried with its owner. Even in the tomb, it shows how emptiness makes things move.

11.caption: A potter shaped this jar more than five thousand years ago. The clay makes the walls; the empty inside makes it useful.
11.look: Follow the black spirals around the belly of the jar. They swirl and turn, almost like water. The painted surface is lovely, but think about the inside, which you cannot see. That hidden space is why the jar was made. It held grain, or water, or seeds for the next year. Chapter 11 says we shape clay into a vessel, and it is the empty space inside that makes it work. The spirals turn around a hollow centre, just as the chapter turns around its central idea.

12.caption: Wang Ximeng's blue and green peaks are dazzling. Laozi warns that the five colours can blind the eye.
12.look: This is a small part of a huge scroll painted by a young court artist in 1113. The mineral blues and greens are brilliant even after nine hundred years. Let yourself enjoy them. Then notice the pull they have on you, the wish to see more and more. Chapter 12 says the five colours blind the eye, the five tones deafen the ear, and the chase drives the heart wild. The sage cares for the belly, not the eye. Close your eyes for a moment after looking. What stays with you?

13.caption: The poet Li Bai, who had both favour and disgrace at court, walks off alone. Liang Kai needs only a few lines.
13.look: Count the strokes. The robe is one long sweep; the head a few quick touches. Li Bai looks up as he walks, chanting a poem to himself. He served at the Tang court, was praised, then sent away. Chapter 13 says that favour and disgrace are both alarming, because both depend on others. The person who values his own body as much as the whole world can be trusted with the world. Liang Kai himself is said to have walked away from the Song painting academy. His Li Bai belongs to nobody. Notice how much blank paper surrounds him.

14.caption: Sesshū's splashed ink barely forms a picture. Look at it and you do not quite see it.
14.look: At first there are only blots and washes of grey. Slowly a rock appears, then a tree, then the roof of a small house with a flag, then mountains so pale they seem breathed onto the paper. Nothing is outlined. Chapter 14 describes the Way as what you look at and do not see, listen to and do not hear, grasp and do not catch. It is shape without shape, image without thing. Let your eyes go soft. The painting comes and goes, as the chapter says the Way does.

15.caption: In Sesshū's winter landscape a sharp line of cliff cuts down through cold air. The ancient masters were careful, as if crossing a winter stream.
15.look: Look at the left scroll first. A single dark stroke runs down the middle like a crack in ice. Beside it, a tiny temple and a figure with a hat move through the snow. Everything is still and alert. Chapter 15 says the ancient masters were hesitant, as if crossing a stream in winter; watchful, as if they feared their neighbours; simple, like uncarved wood; open, like a valley; murky, like muddy water. Then turn to the autumn scroll on the right, softer and wider. Both seasons ask for the same attention.

16.caption: Ni Zan paints an empty pavilion between two shores. Attain the summit of emptiness; hold fast to stillness.
16.look: The picture has three parts: a near bank with thin trees and an empty hut, a wide band of blank water, and low hills far away. No person is present. Ni Zan used dry, light ink and almost no colour. Chapter 16 asks us to reach complete emptiness and keep deep stillness, and to watch the ten thousand things rise and return to their root. Let your eye rest in the empty water. It is the centre of the painting. The hut waits there, like a mind with nothing in it, ready to receive.

17.caption: Fishermen work the river under huge peaks. No ruler appears; the people live their lives and say, "We did this ourselves."
17.look: Find the small boats near the bottom. Then let your eye climb the narrow, steep mountains that rise like folded curtains. The fishermen are tiny, but the painting belongs to them. Nobody commands them. Chapter 17 says the best rulers are those the people barely know exist. When the work is done, the people say it happened by itself. Xu Daoning painted this around 1049, and it has the quiet of evening. Listen for the song in the title. It is the people's song, not the court's.

18.caption: A rubbing of Confucius the great teacher. When the great Way is forgotten, benevolence and righteousness are preached.
18.look: This image was carved in stone after a design by the Tang painter Wu Daozi, then printed by pressing paper on the stone and rubbing it with ink. Look at the dignified figure, the folded hands, the long robe. Confucius taught benevolence, rightness and ritual. Chapter 18 makes a sharp point: these virtues are named and taught only when the Way has already been lost. When families quarrel, people praise filial children. The chapter is not mocking Confucius. It asks what kind of world needs such teachers. Notice the solemn weight of the portrait.

19.caption: A herdsman rides home on his buffalo through snow. Show plainness, embrace the uncarved block, have few desires.
19.look: The herdsman is bundled against the cold, his face hidden, a pole over his shoulder. The buffalo lowers its head and plods. A bare, snow-laden tree leans over them. Nothing here is clever. Chapter 19 says to cast off sageliness and cleverness, and the people will benefit a hundred times; show the plain silk, hold the uncarved block, reduce the self, lessen desire. Li Di's buffalo and rider move as one, at their own pace. Look at the soft grey of the snowy sky and the patient walk home.

20.caption: Liang Kai's immortal stumbles forward, belly out, eyes squinting. Everyone else is bright; I alone am dull.
20.look: Look at how the body is made: a few broad, wet sweeps of ink, with only tiny fine strokes for the face. The figure seems about to fall over or burst out laughing. Chapter 20 is the most personal chapter of the Daodejing. Others are busy and festive, says the speaker; I alone am drifting, like a baby that has not yet smiled. Others have more than enough; I alone seem to have lost something. Yet I value being fed by the mother. Notice how happy this foolish figure looks.

21.caption: Muqi's dragon comes and goes in the clouds. The Way is elusive and vague, and yet within it there is an image.
21.look: Give your eyes time. At first the scroll looks like dark fog. Then a head appears, a claw, a curl of body, and they fade again into the mist. Muqi painted this with soft, wet ink that leaves no hard edges. Chapter 21 says the Way is shadowy and indistinct, yet within it there is form; dark and obscure, yet within it there is essence. The dragon was an old Chinese image for what cannot be pinned down. Confucius used it for Laozi himself. Watch for the moment when the dragon disappears.

21.caption: Juran's title says it all: seeking the Dao in the autumn mountains. Find the small hut in the fold of the hills.
21.look: The hills are built from long, soft strokes like hemp fibres, rounded and calm. Near the middle there is a small hut where two figures sit and talk. That is the seeking. Everything around them is mountain, mist and pine. Chapter 21 says we can know the beginning of all things only through this hidden essence, which is very real and can be trusted. Juran does not paint the answer. He paints the long walk up and the quiet conversation. Let your eye climb slowly, as if you were going to join them.

22.caption: Wen Zhengming's ancient junipers are twisted and knotted. Bent, they stay whole.
22.look: These trees stood in a garden in Suzhou and were already old when Wen Zhengming drew them. Trace one trunk and you lose it among the others. Every branch bends, forks, turns back. Yet the trees are full of life. Chapter 22 begins: what bends stays whole; what is crooked becomes straight; what is hollow is filled; what is worn becomes new. A straight tree is cut for timber. A crooked one is left to grow. Let your eye follow the knots without trying to straighten them.

23.caption: Ma Yuan's Yellow River throws up foam and spray. A whirlwind does not last all morning.
23.look: Watch the big waves rise and crash, then notice the smaller ones already settling at the edges. Ma Yuan's brush moves fast here, with heavy, curling lines. Chapter 23 says that to speak little is natural. A whirlwind does not last all morning; a downpour does not last all day. If even heaven and earth cannot keep up such force for long, how much less can people? Let the noise of the painting rise in you, and then let it fall. Look at the calmer water at the edges.

24.caption: The emperor's horse strains against its post, eyes rolling. One who stands on tiptoe is not steady.
24.look: Night-Shining White was the favourite horse of the Tang emperor Xuanzong. Han Gan shows it tied to a black post, rearing, nostrils wide. All that strength goes nowhere. Chapter 24 says one who stands on tiptoe does not stand firm; one who takes long strides does not go far; one who shows off is not seen clearly. Look at the stamps and inscriptions crowding around the horse: centuries of owners added their seals. The horse is famous and still tied. Compare its tense body to the calm line of the post.

25.caption: Fan Kuan's mountain fills the sky; the travellers below are almost too small to see. Something formless existed before heaven and earth.
25.look: Stand back and let the great mountain wall press toward you. Then search the bottom edge for the travellers and their mules, tiny and patient. The waterfall on the right is a single white thread. Chapter 25 speaks of something formed in chaos before heaven and earth, silent and empty, standing alone and unchanging. We call it the Way, or Great. Humans follow earth, earth follows heaven, heaven follows the Way, the Way follows what is so of itself. This painting places people inside that order, small but walking.

26.caption: The sage travels all day without leaving the baggage cart. Heaviness is the root of lightness.
26.look: Look again at this little bronze cart, solid and low. Its wheels can turn because the box sits firmly on the axle. Chapter 26 says heaviness is the root of lightness, and stillness is the ruler of agitation. The sage travels all day and never leaves his heavy carts behind; even with splendid views, he stays calm and apart. Notice the weight in the bronze, the low centre of gravity, the steady horse. A light, restless ruler loses his root. A grounded one can move far.

27.caption: Ma Yuan's scholar strolls along a spring path. A good walker leaves no tracks.
27.look: The walker is at the lower left, sleeves loose, brushing past willow branches. A servant follows with a qin. Two birds fly up. The rest of the leaf is open space with a short poem. Nothing is forced. Chapter 27 says a good traveller leaves no tracks, a good speaker makes no slips, a good counter needs no tally. The sage is always good at saving people, so no one is thrown away. Look at how lightly the figure moves into the empty right side of the painting, as if he will leave no mark there.

28.caption: Li Tang fills the scroll with pines and valleys. Know the male, keep to the female; be a valley for the world.
28.look: The painting is dense and dark: strong peaks above, deep pines below, a stream running through the gorge. Let your eye drop down from the heights to the low places, where water collects and the wind moves in the pines. Chapter 28 says: know the bright, keep to the dark; know the high, keep to the low; be a valley for the world, and constant virtue will not leave you. You will return to the uncarved block. Notice how the valley floor, not the peak, holds the life of this picture.

29.caption: The ding was the symbol of rule in ancient China. Laozi calls the world a sacred vessel that cannot be grabbed.
29.look: Look at the solid legs, the raised handles, the band of masks around the belly. Ding cauldrons held offerings, and to own the great ding meant to own the kingdom. Chapter 29 warns those who want to take the world and work on it: the world is a sacred vessel. Whoever acts on it ruins it; whoever grabs it loses it. Things sometimes lead and sometimes follow. Notice that this vessel is meant to be filled, carried with care and used in ritual, not seized.

30.caption: A Han stone shows chariots fighting on a bridge. Where armies camp, thorns and brambles grow.
30.look: This rubbing comes from a family shrine of the second century. Look along the long band: horses rearing, chariots crowded on the arch of the bridge, soldiers in the water below. It is energetic and full of noise. Chapter 30 advises those who help rulers with the Way not to use force. Where armies have stayed, thorns grow; after a great war, bad years follow. Gain your goal, and stop. Do not boast. Look at how the fighters are packed so tightly they can hardly move.

31.caption: A Zhou ritual bell. Laozi says a victory should be marked with the rites of mourning.
31.look: This bell was struck in ceremonies nearly three thousand years ago. Look at the rows of knobs, the curved rim, the dragons in low relief. A bell like this sounded at sacrifices and also at funerals. Chapter 31 says weapons are instruments of ill omen; a gentleman uses them only when he must, and values calm. A victory is not beautiful. Those who rejoice in killing cannot win the world. After a battle, the dead should be mourned and the victory treated as a funeral. Imagine the bell's long, low note.

32.caption: Dong Yuan's soft hills curve around a wide river. The Way in the world is like streams flowing to rivers and the sea.
32.look: Follow the river from the far distance toward the shore, where boats gather and people wait. The hills are round and gentle, painted in long, soft strokes. Chapter 32 says the Way, constant and nameless, is like the uncarved block. If rulers could keep it, all things would come of themselves, and the sweet dew would fall without being commanded. The Way in the world is like small streams flowing into the rivers and the sea. Notice how every line in this landscape leads toward the water.

33.caption: A small figure sits alone beside a stream under dark mountains. One who knows himself is enlightened.
33.look: Find the seated figure near the bottom. He looks out at the water, his back to the high cliffs. He is not climbing or travelling. Chapter 33 says: one who knows others is clever; one who knows himself is enlightened. One who conquers others is strong; one who conquers himself is mighty. One who knows when he has enough is rich. Stay with the man by the stream. The great mountain behind him does not distract him. What is he looking at?

34.caption: Dong Yuan's river winds left and right through the scroll. The great Way flows everywhere.
34.look: Trace the water from the top of the scroll to the bottom. It turns this way and that, wind-blown, never in a straight line. Mountains, a house and trees all lean along its course. Chapter 34 says the great Way flows everywhere, to the left and to the right. All things depend on it, and it does not refuse them. It completes its work and claims nothing. Because it never makes itself great, it can be great. Let your eye drift with the current.

35.caption: Under a pine, a man plays the qin while two officials listen. Music and good food make travellers stop; the Way has no flavour.
35.look: The player sits with his head bowed toward the strings. The listener in green looks down; the one in red looks up and away. A small incense burner stands on a stand. Chapter 35 says music and fine food make passing travellers stop, but the Way, when spoken, is bland and has no flavour. Look at it and it is not enough to see; listen and it is not enough to hear; use it and it never runs out. The qin's music was quiet and plain. Notice the stillness of the three men.

36.caption: Bada Shanren's small fish swims under a heavy rock. Fish should not leave the deep water.
36.look: The rock at the top seems about to fall. Below, a fish with a round, staring eye floats in open space. Bada Shanren was a member of the Ming royal family who became a monk after the dynasty fell; his fish and birds often look sideways at the world. Chapter 36 says the soft and weak overcome the hard and strong. Fish should not leave the depths; the sharp tools of a state should not be shown. Notice how much empty paper surrounds the fish. It is safe there.

37.caption: Tōhaku's pines appear and disappear in fog. The Way does nothing, yet nothing is left undone.
37.look: This is one screen of a pair. Stand back. The pines seem to come forward and sink back as mist moves through them. Some are painted with dark, fast strokes; others are only a breath of grey. Much of the screen is empty paper. Chapter 37 says the Way never acts, yet nothing is left undone. If rulers could hold to it, all things would transform themselves. Without desire there is stillness, and the world settles of itself. Let your eye stay in the fog between the trees.

38.caption: A Han rubbing of Confucius visiting Laozi to ask about the rites. Laozi says ritual is the thin husk of loyalty.
38.look: Look for the two figures facing each other in the centre of the band. Around them stand students and attendants, all in the formal pose of a meeting. The story was popular on Han tomb carvings: the great teacher of ritual coming to learn from the archivist of Zhou. Chapter 38 says high virtue is not conscious of itself, and so it has virtue. When the Way is lost, virtue appears; then benevolence, then righteousness, then ritual, which is the thin edge of loyalty and the beginning of disorder. The great person stays with the fruit, not the flower.

39.caption: The cong is round inside and square outside, a joining of heaven and earth. Everything that attains the One is whole.
39.look: Look at the tall, dark green tube. The outer corners are square; the hole through its centre is round. In early China, round stood for heaven and square for earth. Chapter 39 says that in ancient times, heaven attained the One and became clear, earth attained the One and became steady, valleys attained the One and became full. The ruler takes the lowly as his root. Do not wish to jingle like jade; be rough like stone. Notice that this jade is not glittering. It is plain, heavy and quiet.

40.caption: One of the earliest printed yin-yang swirls, from about 1370. Returning is the movement of the Way.
40.look: Look at the black and white halves turning around each other. Each carries a small dot of the other. Around the circle are the names of the eight trigrams. Zhao Huiqian called this the River Chart of Heaven and Earth. Chapter 40 is very short: returning is the movement of the Way; weakness is the use of the Way. The ten thousand things are born from being, and being is born from non-being. Follow the curve with your eye. It never stops; it always comes back.

41.caption: The eccentric monk with his broom laughs at the world. If the lowest kind of student did not laugh, it would not be the Way.
41.look: Indara drew this figure with a few loose, almost careless strokes. The broom, the tattered robe and the open mouth are all you need. Hanshan and Shide were Tang dynasty eccentrics who lived at a temple, wrote poems on rocks and laughed at monks and officials alike. Chapter 41 says when the best students hear of the Way, they practise it; when the middle ones hear of it, they half believe; when the worst hear of it, they laugh out loud. The great image has no shape. Look at the joy in this ragged figure.

42.caption: A Daoist diagram shows the One dividing into many and returning. The Way gives birth to one, one to two, two to three, three to all things.
42.look: Diagrams like this were used in inner alchemy, the Daoist practice of refining the body and spirit. Look at the rings, the labels, the way the parts are counted outward and drawn back to the centre. Chapter 42 gives the famous sequence: the Way produces one, one produces two, two produces three, and three produces the ten thousand things. All things carry yin on their backs and hold yang in their arms, and blending breath makes them harmonious. Let your eye move from the centre outward and back again.

43.caption: A scholar watches a waterfall pour through the rocks. The softest thing in the world rides over the hardest.
43.look: Find the white line of water falling from the cliff, then the scholar on the rock, quiet and attentive. The pine leans across the leaf. Chapter 43 says the softest thing in the world overcomes the hardest; what has no substance enters where there is no gap. From this I know the value of non-action. Few in the world reach the teaching without words. The scholar does not speak. He watches water do what it has always done: wear away stone by never stopping.

43.caption: A Han tomb carving of a butcher at work, often linked with Zhuangzi's Cook Ding. No-thickness enters where there is space.
43.look: This is a kitchen scene, not a portrait of Cook Ding himself, but it shows the same work. Look at the figure bending to the hanging carcass, the robed man standing by. In Zhuangzi's story the cook's knife never dulls because it slides through the empty spaces in the joints. Chapter 43 says what has no substance enters where there is no gap. Imagine the edge moving through the ox without force. See the story "Cook Ding Carves an Ox".

44.caption: A fisherman floats on calm water, far from court. Which is dearer, fame or your life?
44.look: The boat is very small. Above it, a poem by the painter praises the fisherman's life. Wu Zhen was a Yuan dynasty recluse who painted fishermen again and again; for him, the fisherman meant a person who has chosen freedom over office. Chapter 44 asks: fame or the self, which is dearer? The self or possessions, which is more? Gain or loss, which harms more? One who knows what is enough is not disgraced; one who knows when to stop is not in danger. Look at the stillness of the water.

45.caption: Mi Fu's cursive looks careless and spills across the page. The greatest skill seems clumsy.
45.look: Look at one character and you may not recognise it. The strokes run together, thicken, thin out, and rush on. Mi Fu was a master of every script, yet in his cursive writing he lets the brush seem almost out of control. Chapter 45 says great completion seems incomplete, yet its use is never exhausted. Great fullness seems empty. Great straightness seems bent; great skill seems clumsy; great eloquence seems to stammer. Follow one line from top to bottom without trying to read it. Feel the speed and the pauses.

46.caption: Li Gonglin's horse stands calmly with its groom. When the world has the Way, horses fertilise the fields.
46.look: Li Gonglin drew this horse with fine, plain ink lines and almost no colour. The animal is quiet and powerful. The groom holds the reins loosely. Chapter 46 says when the world has the Way, fast horses are sent back to haul dung in the fields. When the world lacks the Way, war horses are bred on the frontier. No disaster is greater than not knowing what is enough. Look at the horse's calm eye and soft stance. It is not running anywhere. This is a horse at peace.

47.caption: A scholar sits under a pine and listens to the wind. Without going out the door, one can know the world.
47.look: The man leans back against the roots, eyes half closed. Above him, the pine twists high into the scroll. A stream runs nearby. He is not travelling or studying. He is listening. Chapter 47 says: without going out the door, know the world; without looking out the window, see the way of heaven. The further you go, the less you know. Imagine the sound the scholar hears. Let the painting go quiet in your mind until only the wind in the pines is left.

48.caption: The eighth of the Ten Oxherding Pictures is an empty circle. In pursuing the Way, one loses a little every day.
48.look: In the earlier pictures of this series, a herdsman searches for an ox, catches it, tames it, rides it home. Then, in the eighth, both the ox and the man are gone. Only the circle remains. Chapter 48 says those who study gain more every day; those who follow the Way lose more every day. Lose and lose again, until you reach non-action. Do nothing, and nothing is left undone. Look into the circle. There is nothing to find there, and nothing missing.

49.caption: A girl and her small brother play with a cat under winter blossoms. The sage treats all people as his children.
49.look: The children wear fine clothes and hold a peacock-feather banner. The girl bends gently toward her brother. A cat watches them. Plum and camellia bloom against the cold. Chapter 49 says the sage has no fixed heart of his own; he takes the hearts of the people as his heart. He is good to the good and also good to those who are not good. In the world he is calm and unbiased; the people turn their eyes and ears to him, and he treats them all as children. Notice the girl's care.

50.caption: Muqi's tiger crouches in the grass. One who cares well for life meets no tiger on the road.
50.look: Look first at the eyes, then at the soft, wet ink of the body. The tiger is powerful but not attacking. Chapter 50 says among those who go out into life and into death, some are companions of life, some companions of death. Those who care well for life walk without meeting rhinoceros or tiger. Their bodies offer no place for the claw or the horn. Why? Because they have no place of death. Look at the tiger. It is not looking for you.

51.caption: Guo Xi's mountains seem to stir as spring begins. The Way gives birth; virtue nourishes.
51.look: The whole scroll twists upward like steam: rocks curl, trees reach, mist lifts. Look at the fishermen and travellers in the lower corners, small signs of human life waking up with the season. Chapter 51 says the Way gives birth to all things, virtue nourishes them, matter shapes them, circumstances complete them. The Way gives birth and does not possess; it acts and does not rely; it raises and does not rule. This is called mysterious virtue. Spring does all its work and asks nothing in return.

52.caption: Shitao's traveller sits in a small boat on blank water, going home. Know the child; return to the mother.
52.look: The painting is mostly empty. The man in the boat sits quietly; reeds lean at the bottom, a few soft hills appear far above. Chapter 52 says the world has a beginning, which is its mother. Knowing the mother, you know the child; knowing the child, return to the mother, and to the end of your life you will be safe. Block the openings, close the doors, and you will not be worn out. See the small and call it clear. The boat is moving home. Let it.

53.caption: Emperor Huizong painted cranes over his palace as a sign of good fortune. Fifteen years later his dynasty fell.
53.look: The blue is intense, the cranes elegant, the roof precise. This was painted by an emperor who loved art and luxury. In 1127 his capital fell to invaders and he died a captive. Chapter 53 says the great Way is very level, but people love side paths. The court is very fine, the fields full of weeds, the granaries empty; people wear rich clothes and carry sharp swords, eat and drink too much, have more wealth than they need. This is called robbery. Look at the beauty, and remember the fields.

54.caption: Two old pines stand together, deeply rooted. What is well planted cannot be uprooted.
54.look: Follow each trunk down to the ground. The roots grip the earth; the branches twist but hold. Behind them, a stream and soft hills. Wu Zhen painted this in 1328. Chapter 54 says what is well planted is not uprooted, what is well embraced does not slip away. Cultivate it in yourself, and virtue is real; in your family, and it is abundant; in your village, and it lasts long. Look at how the two trees lean together. They are rooted, and they are companions.

55.caption: Two children bend over their game in an autumn garden. One who holds virtue fully is like a newborn child.
55.look: Look past the tall garden rock and the flowers to the children at the round stools. Their heads are close together. They do not notice anything else. Chapter 55 says one rich in virtue is like a newborn. Wasps and snakes do not bite it; wild beasts do not attack it. Its bones are soft, its muscles weak, yet its grip is firm. It cries all day and does not grow hoarse: its harmony is perfect. Notice how relaxed the children's bodies are, and how completely they attend.

56.caption: Zhou Dongqing's carp turn among water plants, free and at ease. Those who know do not speak.
56.look: This scroll is called The Pleasures of Fishes, after the story of Zhuangzi and Huizi on the bridge over the Hao River. Look at the big carp curving upward, its body light in the water. The plants move with the current. Chapter 56 says those who know do not speak; those who speak do not know. Block the openings, blunt the sharpness, untie the knots, soften the glare, become one with the dust. This is called mysterious sameness. The fish are not explaining their joy. See the story "The Happy Fish of the Hao River".

57.caption: Huang Gongwang's long scroll of quiet hills shows people living by the river. I do nothing, and the people transform themselves.
57.look: The brushwork is dry and light; nothing shouts. Follow the riverbank, the pines, the small houses. Huang Gongwang worked on this scroll for several years, adding a little at a time when the mood came. Chapter 57 says the more prohibitions there are, the poorer the people; the more sharp weapons, the more trouble; the more laws, the more thieves. So the sage says: I do nothing, and the people change by themselves. I love stillness, and they become upright. Look at how the painting seems to unroll on its own.

58.caption: A groom stands calmly beside his horse. Misfortune is what fortune leans on; fortune is where misfortune hides.
58.look: The man and the horse stand side by side, neither leading. Zhao Mengfu painted this in 1296. He was a descendant of the Song royal house who served the Mongol emperors, a choice that brought him both honour and criticism. Chapter 58 says misfortune is where good fortune rests; good fortune is where misfortune hides. Who knows where it ends? There is no fixed right. Look at the calm face of the groom. He does not know whether this horse will bring good or bad luck. See the story "The Old Man at the Frontier Loses His Horse".

59.caption: An old plum branch, gnarled and spare, still flowers. In caring for people and serving heaven, nothing is better than frugality.
59.look: The branch is crooked and rough, with only a few blossoms. Chen Hongshou leaves most of the leaf empty. Old plum trees were admired in China because they bloom in the cold, on wood that looks dead. Chapter 59 says in governing people and serving heaven, nothing is better than frugality. Being frugal means preparing early; it builds up virtue. This is called deep roots and firm stem, the way to long life and lasting vision. Look at the thin branch holding its flowers.

60.caption: Goldfish turn and drift among the plants. Govern a great state as you cook a small fish: gently, and not too much stirring.
60.look: Look at how each fish moves in its own direction, some up, some down, all at ease. Nothing disturbs the water. Chapter 60 begins with a famous image: govern a great state as you would cook a small fish. Stir it too much and it falls apart. When the world is governed by the Way, even the spirits lose their power to harm. Let your eye drift with the fish. The painter has not crowded them or ordered them in lines. Each finds its own place.

61.caption: The Tang emperor receives an envoy from Tibet. A great state should be like the low place where rivers meet.
61.look: On the right, the emperor sits in a litter carried by court ladies. On the left, an official in red, the Tibetan envoy and an interpreter stand with hands folded. This meeting led to a marriage alliance. Chapter 61 says a great state is like the lower reaches of a river, where all streams meet; it is the female of the world. The female overcomes the male by stillness, by taking the lower place. A great state gains small states by lowering itself. Look at the calm, unhurried gestures.

62.caption: A jade bi disc, a treasure offered to heaven. Better than jade and fine horses is to sit still and offer the Way.
62.look: Look at the round disc with its round hole. Bi discs were laid in tombs and offered in rituals to heaven. They were among the most precious things a ruler could give. Chapter 62 says the Way is the hidden treasure of all things. When a new emperor is crowned, rather than offering a jade disc followed by a team of four horses, it is better to sit still and offer this Way. Why did the ancients value it? Because with it, those who seek will find, and those who err are forgiven.

63.caption: A plain white Ding ware bowl. Taste the tasteless; do great things while they are small.
63.look: The bowl has no painted decoration, only the soft cream of its glaze and the line of its rim. Song connoisseurs loved Ding ware for exactly this restraint. Chapter 63 says: act without acting, work without working, taste the tasteless. Handle the difficult while it is easy; do the great while it is small. All difficult things in the world start from easy ones. The sage never tries to do great things, and so achieves greatness. Look at the simple curve of the bowl. Nothing here is hard, and nothing is missing.

64.caption: A lone figure walks under bare autumn trees. A journey of a thousand li begins beneath your feet.
64.look: Find the small walker at the bottom of the scroll. Above him, tall bare trees rise and birds lift into the air. Wen Zhengming painted this in 1554, when he was in his eighties. Chapter 64 says a tree you can barely circle with your arms grew from a tiny shoot; a tower of nine storeys rises from a heap of earth; a journey of a thousand li begins with the ground beneath your feet. Look at the walker's next step. The whole journey is there.

65.caption: A dwelling hidden deep in the mountains, far from clever government. The ancients did not make people sharp but kept them simple.
65.look: Look again for the little house in the folds of rock. It is protected, unseen, not displayed. Chapter 65 says those who practised the Way in ancient times did not use it to make the people clever, but to keep them simple. People are hard to govern when they have too much cunning. Governing by cleverness harms the state; governing without it blesses the state. This is deep and far-reaching virtue; it turns things around and leads back to great harmony. Notice how far the house is from any road.

66.caption: Long swells of the sea under rising mist. Rivers and seas rule a hundred valleys because they lie lower.
66.look: The waves here are broad and slow, rolling across the bottom of the leaf. Above them, cloud rises into empty golden silk. All the water in the world ends here. Chapter 66 says rivers and seas can be kings of the hundred valleys because they are good at staying low. So the sage, wishing to be above the people, speaks humbly; wishing to lead them, walks behind. He is on top, and the people do not feel his weight. Let your eye sink to the bottom of the painting and rest.

67.caption: Laozi rides slowly past bamboo on his ox. I have three treasures: compassion, frugality, and not daring to be first.
67.look: Chen Hongshou gives Laozi a gentle, slightly strange face and a calm ox. He sits loosely, in no hurry, as if the road will wait. Bamboo bends behind him. Chapter 67 is one of the few places where the speaker says "I" so plainly: I have three treasures that I hold and keep. The first is compassion, the second is frugality, the third is not daring to be first in the world. Compassion makes courage possible. Look at the old man's relaxed hands. Nothing about him pushes forward.

68.caption: Hakuin's Bodhidharma stares out with wide eyes but does not move. The best warrior is not warlike.
68.look: This huge face is made of a few thick, wet strokes; the robe is one bold sweep. The inscription above says, roughly, "Point straight at the human heart; see your nature and become Buddha." Bodhidharma's stare is fierce, yet he sits completely still. Chapter 68 says the best warrior is not warlike, the best fighter is not angry, the best winner does not engage. This is the virtue of not contending. Compare the gamecock in Zhuangzi that became like wood. See the story "The Gamecock Like Wood".

69.caption: Look again at the Han battle on the bridge. Military strategists say: I would rather be the guest than the host.
69.look: This time, notice the moments of retreat in the crowd: horses turning, figures falling back toward the river. Chapter 69 quotes the strategists: I dare not be the host but rather the guest; I dare not advance an inch but rather retreat a foot. This is called moving without moving, rolling up the sleeve without baring the arm. No disaster is greater than underestimating the enemy. When equal armies meet, the side that grieves will win. Look for the stillness hidden inside the struggle.

70.caption: Old Laozi rides his buffalo while a boy walks beside him. My words are easy to understand, yet few understand them.
70.look: This later painting shows Laozi as Daoist tradition remembered him: white beard, high forehead, kind face, the water buffalo, and a young follower carrying a gourd. Chapter 70 is Laozi speaking about himself: my words are very easy to know and very easy to practise, yet no one in the world can know them or practise them. Those who know me are few. So the sage wears coarse cloth and carries jade inside it. Look at the plainness of his travelling. See the story "Bian He's Uncut Jade".

71.caption: Huike cuts off his arm to show Bodhidharma he is sincere. To know that you do not know is highest.
71.look: Bodhidharma sits facing the cave wall, drawn in a pale, firm outline. He does not turn. Behind him, Huike holds out his arm, his face tense. Sesshū painted this at seventy-six. The story says Huike asked to have his mind put at rest, and Bodhidharma said, "Bring me your mind." Huike said, "I have searched, and I cannot find it." Chapter 71 says to know that you do not know is the best; not to know that you do not know is a sickness. Look at the great blank face of the wall.

72.caption: A man with a staff crosses a little bridge toward his cottage. Do not crowd people's dwellings; do not weary their lives.
72.look: The cottage sits among pines; the hills are soft and rounded. The walker moves slowly. Shen Zhou spent most of his life at home in the countryside near Suzhou and refused official posts. Chapter 72 says when people do not fear authority, something terrible will come. Do not narrow where they live; do not oppress their livelihood. If you do not oppress them, they will not tire of you. The sage knows himself but does not display himself. Look at the small, safe world this man is walking into.

73.caption: A Tang dynasty star chart from Dunhuang maps the sky around the pole. Heaven's net is vast; its mesh is wide, yet nothing slips through.
73.look: Look at the dots and lines: each group is a constellation, carefully named. This chart, made around 700 CE, is one of the oldest star maps in the world. The stars seem scattered and far apart, yet they turn together around the still pole, night after night. Chapter 73 says the Way of heaven does not contend yet wins well, does not speak yet answers well, is not summoned yet comes, is calm yet plans well. Heaven's net is wide and loose, yet nothing is lost. Look at the spaces between the stars.

74.caption: A Han kitchen carving shows the butcher's work. One who cuts in place of the master carpenter rarely escapes hurting his hand.
74.look: Look at the butcher's bent body and the heavy carcass. This was skilled, dangerous work, best left to those who knew it. Chapter 74 says if people do not fear death, how can you threaten them with death? There is always a master executioner, which is heaven itself. To kill in its place is like cutting wood in place of the master carpenter: you will rarely avoid cutting your own hand. Notice how carefully the worker stands. His tool is not a weapon. See the story "Cook Ding Carves an Ox".

75.caption: Farm families give thanks after the harvest. People starve when those above eat too much in taxes.
75.look: This print comes from a set of pictures of farming and weaving made for the Kangxi emperor in 1696. Look at the families bowing in the yard, the thatched roofs, the bare trees. The grain on which the empire lived came from houses like these. Chapter 75 says the people are hungry because those above eat too much tax. The people are hard to govern because those above interfere. They take death lightly because those above seek life too richly. Look at the humble offering, and ask who should be giving thanks to whom.

76.caption: Old trees twist beside a cold waterfall. Living things are soft and supple; dead things are hard and dry.
76.look: Look at the trees: some branches still bend and leaf; others are stiff and broken. The waterfall slides down between them, thin and endless. Two small figures stand at the bottom, listening. Chapter 76 says people are soft and weak when born, hard and stiff when dead. Plants are tender and supple when alive, dry and brittle when dead. So the hard and strong are companions of death; the soft and weak are companions of life. A rigid army is defeated; a rigid tree is cut. Compare the water to the dead wood.

77.caption: A carved Han stone in three bands: deities, a chariot, a hunt. The Way of heaven is like stretching a bow: lower the high, raise the low.
77.look: Read the slab from top to bottom. The upper band shows seated figures of the spirit world; the middle a chariot and attendants; the lowest a hunt with running animals. Archers and hunters in Han carvings draw bows with their whole body. Chapter 77 says the Way of heaven is like drawing a bow: the high end is pulled down, the low end raised; what has too much is reduced, what has too little is filled. The way of people is different: they take from those who lack to give to those who have more. Look for balance in the bands.

78.caption: Ma Yuan's autumn water spreads in endless small waves. Nothing in the world is softer than water, yet nothing is better at wearing down the hard.
78.look: Look at the patient rhythm of the waves, row after row, like woven cloth. No single wave is strong. Yet the whole surface moves with great power. Chapter 78 says nothing under heaven is softer or weaker than water, yet for attacking the hard and strong nothing can surpass it, because nothing can take its place. Everyone knows that the weak overcome the strong and the soft overcome the hard, yet no one can practise it. Straight words seem crooked. Let your eye ride the waves to the far edge.

79.caption: Bamboo slips from a Chu tomb, the kind of writing material on which the earliest Daodejing copies survive. The sage holds the left half of the tally and does not press for payment.
79.look: Look at the narrow strips laid side by side, each with a single column of small characters. Contracts and debts in ancient China were often written on split tallies; each side kept half. The oldest known manuscripts of Laozi, found at Guodian in 1993, were written on slips like these. Chapter 79 says after a great quarrel is settled, some resentment always remains. So the sage holds the left half of the tally but makes no demands on others. The Way of heaven has no favourites; it is always with the good. Notice the patient handwriting.

80.caption: A fisherman finds a hidden valley where people have lived in peace for centuries. Small country, few people.
80.look: Follow the stream into the scroll as the fisherman did. Blue-green hills and blossoming trees close around the water. Chapter 80 imagines a small state with few people. They have tools but do not use them, boats and carts but do not ride them, weapons but do not display them. They find their food sweet, their clothes beautiful, their homes peaceful, their customs pleasant. Neighbouring villages are so close that they can hear each other's roosters and dogs, yet people grow old and die without visiting. See the story "The Peach Blossom Spring".

80.caption: Cai Jia paints the hidden valley in a tall scroll of mist and peach blossom. Look for the fisherman's boat.
80.look: Begin at the bottom, where the stream and the boat appear. Then climb past the peach grove into the misty peaks. The entrance to the valley is hard to see; that is the point of the story. Nobody could ever find it again. Chapter 80 describes a life so content that no one wants to travel or conquer. Cai Jia's painting gives you only a glimpse of that world, half hidden in cloud. Let your eye search for the opening between the rocks, and then let it go.

81.caption: Zhang Lu's Laozi rides away on his ox, looking up from his book. True words are not beautiful; beautiful words are not true.
81.look: The old man's head is high and bald; his eyes are lifted, perhaps to the sky, perhaps to the road ahead. The ox steps forward with lowered horns. Zhang Lu paints with quick, rough strokes, nothing polished. Chapter 81 is the last chapter: true words are not beautiful; good people do not argue; those who know are not learned. The sage does not hoard. The more he does for others, the more he has; the more he gives, the more he gains. Laozi leaves, and the book stays. See the story "The Keeper of the Pass".

hangu-pass.title: The Keeper of the Pass
hangu-pass.text:
Laozi kept the archives of the Zhou court for many years. He watched the dynasty grow weak and its rulers quarrel, and at last he decided to leave. He set out to the west, an old man on a slow animal, and came to the Hangu Pass, the gate between the heartland and the wild country beyond.

The keeper of the pass was a man named Yin Xi. Later tradition says that Yin Xi had read the sky, seen a purple vapour drift in from the east, and known that a sage was coming. When the old traveller arrived, Yin Xi would not simply wave him through. "You are about to go into retirement," he said. "Before you go, write a book for me."

Laozi had spent his life refusing to put the Way into words. He had told Confucius that the words of the ancients were only the footprints of men whose bones had long since rotted. Yet he stayed at the pass, and he wrote. The book was in two parts, one on the Way and one on its Power, a little more than five thousand characters in all.

Then he handed it to the keeper, rode on through the gate, and went west. The historian Sima Qian ends the story very simply: "No one knows where he died."

The book stayed behind. The man who wrote it did not.

dragon.title: Confucius Meets a Dragon
dragon.text:
When Confucius was still a young teacher, he travelled to the Zhou capital to ask the archivist Laozi about the rites of the ancient kings. He came with questions about ceremonies, ancestors, and the conduct of a gentleman.

Laozi did not answer the questions. "The men you talk about," he said, "have turned to dust with their bones. Only their words are left. When a gentleman finds his time, he rides in a carriage. When he does not, he drifts like a tumbleweed in the wind. I have heard that a good merchant hides his goods so that his shop seems empty, and that a man of full virtue looks like a fool. Put away your proud airs and your many wishes, your eager manner and your ambitions. None of them helps you. That is all I have to tell you."

Confucius went back to his students and said nothing for three days. At last they asked him what he had learned.

"A bird, I know, can fly," he said. "A fish, I know, can swim. A beast, I know, can run. What runs can be caught in a net. What swims can be caught on a line. What flies can be brought down with an arrow. But the dragon? I do not know how it rides the wind and the clouds up into the sky. Today I met Laozi. He is like a dragon."

cook-ding.title: Cook Ding Carves an Ox
cook-ding.text:
Cook Ding was cutting up an ox for Lord Wenhui. Wherever his hand touched, wherever his shoulder leaned, wherever his foot stepped, wherever his knee pressed, the flesh fell away with a soft hiss. The knife moved with a rhythm, as if he were dancing an old court dance to old court music.

"Wonderful!" said the lord. "How can skill reach such a level?"

The cook put down his knife. "What I care about is the Way, which goes beyond skill. When I began, I saw nothing but the whole ox. After three years I no longer saw the whole ox. Now I meet it with my spirit, not with my eyes. My senses stop, and the spirit moves where it wants. I follow the natural lines, slip into the big gaps, and guide the blade along the hollows. I never touch a tendon, still less a bone.

"A good cook changes his knife once a year, because he cuts. An ordinary cook changes it once a month, because he hacks. I have had this knife for nineteen years. It has cut up thousands of oxen, and its edge is as fresh as if it had just come from the whetstone. The joints have spaces, and the blade has no thickness. When something with no thickness enters where there is space, there is more than enough room for it to play.

"Still, when I come to a knot, I see the difficulty. I grow careful. My eyes stop, I move slowly, and the knife barely stirs. Then, with a quiet sound, the thing comes apart like earth falling to the ground. I stand with the knife in my hand, look around, and feel content. Then I wipe the blade and put it away."

"Excellent," said Lord Wenhui. "From the words of Cook Ding I have learned how to nourish life."

butterfly.title: The Butterfly Dream
butterfly.text:
Once Zhuang Zhou dreamed that he was a butterfly. He fluttered here and there, a butterfly in every way, happy and doing as he pleased. He did not know that he was Zhuang Zhou.

Suddenly he woke up. There he was, solid and unmistakable, Zhuang Zhou lying on his mat.

But now he did not know: was he Zhuang Zhou, who had dreamed he was a butterfly? Or was he a butterfly, now dreaming that it was Zhuang Zhou?

Between Zhuang Zhou and the butterfly there must be some difference. This, Zhuangzi says, is what we call the transformation of things.

The story is very short, and it does not end with a lesson. It leaves the reader in the moment just after waking, when the edges of the self are still soft. The Daodejing says that being and non-being give birth to each other, that long and short shape each other. Here the dreamer and the dreamed do the same.

useless-tree.title: The Useless Tree
useless-tree.source: Zhuangzi ch.4 (Renjian shi) and ch.1 (Xiaoyao you)
useless-tree.text:
A carpenter named Shi was travelling to the state of Qi. At Crooked Shaft he saw an oak that served as the shrine tree of the village. It was so large that several thousand oxen could rest in its shade. Its trunk was a hundred spans around. Its lowest branches began high above the hilltops, and a dozen of them were big enough to make boats. Crowds came to look at it as if it were a market.

The carpenter did not even turn his head. His apprentice ran after him. "Since I took up the axe I have never seen timber like this. Why will you not look at it?"

"Stop," said Shi. "It is worthless wood. Make a boat from it and the boat sinks. Make a coffin and it rots. Make a tool and it breaks. Make a door and it oozes sap. Make a pillar and the worms eat it. It has no use. That is why it has lived so long."

That night the oak appeared to him in a dream. "What will you compare me with? With your useful trees? The pear, the orange, the pomelo: as soon as their fruit is ripe, they are stripped and broken. Their usefulness makes their lives bitter. They do not live out the years Heaven gave them. For a long time I have tried to be useless. Now that I am near death, I have managed it, and that is my great use. If I had been useful, would I ever have grown this big? And you, a useless man near death, how can you know what a useless tree is?"

When the carpenter woke, he told his dream. "If it wants to be useless," asked the apprentice, "why is it a shrine tree?"

"Hush," said the carpenter. "It only pretends."

gourd.title: Huizi's Giant Gourd
gourd.text:
Huizi, Zhuangzi's friend and favourite opponent in argument, came to him with a complaint.

"The King of Wei gave me the seeds of a great gourd. I planted them, and the gourd grew so big that it held five piculs. I filled it with water, but it was too heavy to lift. I cut it in half to make ladles, but they were too wide and flat to dip into anything. It was huge, certainly, but it was no use. So I smashed it to pieces."

"You are clumsy with big things," said Zhuangzi. "In Song there was a family that made a salve to stop hands from chapping. For generations they used it in their trade of bleaching silk in the river. A stranger heard about it and offered them a hundred pieces of gold for the recipe. The family agreed: they had never earned more than a few coins from it. The stranger took the salve to the King of Wu, who was at war with Yue. In winter he led the Wu navy, and his sailors' hands did not crack in the cold water. Wu crushed Yue, and the stranger was given a fief.

"The salve was the same. One man got a fief from it; the others never stopped bleaching silk. The difference was in how they used it.

"You had a gourd that held five piculs. Why not tie it to your waist as a great float and drift across the rivers and lakes? Instead you worried that it was too wide to hold anything. Your mind still has a lot of underbrush in it."

frog-well.title: The Frog in the Old Well
frog-well.text:
A frog lived in a broken-down well. One day he called out to a great turtle from the Eastern Sea.

"What a happy life I have! When I go out, I hop along the rim of the well. When I come in, I rest in the gaps of the broken bricks. I swim, and the water holds me up under my arms and chin. I dive into the mud, and it covers my feet. I look at the shrimps and the crabs and the tadpoles, and none of them can match me. To have a whole pool of water to myself, to sit astride a whole broken well: this is the best of joys! Why don't you come in and see?"

The turtle tried. But before he had put his left foot in, his right knee was already stuck. He backed out carefully and began to describe the sea.

"A distance of a thousand li does not tell you how wide it is. A height of a thousand fathoms does not tell you how deep it is. In the time of Yu there were floods nine years out of ten, and the sea did not rise. In the time of Tang there was drought seven years out of eight, and its shores did not fall. It does not change for a short time or a long time. It does not grow or shrink for much rain or little. That is the great joy of the Eastern Sea."

The frog in the well heard this. He was astonished, and very small, and he did not know what to do with himself.

hao-river.title: The Happy Fish of the Hao River
hao-river.text:
Zhuangzi and Huizi were strolling on the bridge over the Hao River.

"See how the minnows dart out and swim around so freely," said Zhuangzi. "That is the happiness of fish."

"You are not a fish," said Huizi. "How do you know what makes fish happy?"

"You are not me," said Zhuangzi. "How do you know that I don't know what makes fish happy?"

"I am not you," said Huizi, "so of course I don't know what you know. But you are certainly not a fish, so it is complete: you don't know the happiness of fish."

"Let's go back to where we started," said Zhuangzi. "You said, 'How do you know what makes fish happy?' You asked me that because you already knew that I knew it. I knew it here, standing above the Hao."

Huizi wins the argument on logic. Zhuangzi does not try to beat him on logic. He simply points back to the bridge, the water, and the small silver fish in it. Knowing happens there, in the meeting, before anyone starts to argue about it.

hundun.title: The Death of Hundun
hundun.text:
The emperor of the Southern Sea was called Shu, which means Quick. The emperor of the Northern Sea was called Hu, which means Sudden. The emperor of the Centre was called Hundun, which means Chaos, or the Undivided Lump.

From time to time Shu and Hu met in Hundun's land, and Hundun always treated them very kindly. Shu and Hu talked about how they could repay his goodness.

"All men have seven openings," they said, "so that they can see, hear, eat, and breathe. Hundun alone has none. Let's try boring some for him."

So every day they bored one hole. On the seventh day, Hundun died.

This is the last story in the Inner Chapters of the Zhuangzi. The two visitors mean well. They want to give their friend what they themselves have: eyes and ears and a mouth, a way to take in the world in separate pieces. But Hundun was whole because he was not divided. The Daodejing says that the five colours blind the eye and the five tones deafen the ear. It speaks of returning to the uncarved block. Hundun is that block, and kindness of the wrong kind cut it apart.

lost-pearl.title: The Yellow Emperor's Lost Pearl
lost-pearl.text:
The Yellow Emperor went travelling north of the Red Water. He climbed the Kunlun Mountains and looked out to the south. On his way home, he lost his dark pearl.

He sent Knowledge to look for it, and Knowledge could not find it. He sent Li Zhu, whose eyes were so sharp that he could see the tip of a hair at a hundred paces, and Li Zhu could not find it. He sent Debate, the clever talker, and Debate could not find it.

At last he sent Xiangwang, whose name means something like Shapeless or Without-Image. Xiangwang found it.

"How strange," said the Yellow Emperor. "Of all of them, only Shapeless could find it."

The dark pearl is the Way itself: the dark, round, quiet centre of things. Cleverness does not reach it. Keen sight does not reach it. Fine speech does not reach it. The one who finds it is the one who has no fixed shape and makes no effort to grasp. In the Daodejing, the Way is "looked at but not seen," "listened to but not heard," "grasped at but not caught." Its finder must be the same.

sai-weng.title: The Old Man at the Frontier Loses His Horse
sai-weng.text:
Near the northern frontier lived an old man who was skilled in reading the signs of things. One day, for no reason, his horse ran away into the lands of the northern tribes. His neighbours came to console him.

"How do you know this is not a blessing?" said the old man.

Some months later, the horse came home, and it brought a fine horse of the northern breed with it. The neighbours came to congratulate him.

"How do you know this is not a misfortune?" said the old man.

Now the family had good horses, and the old man's son loved to ride. He fell from the new horse and broke his thigh bone. The neighbours came to console him.

"How do you know this is not a blessing?" said the old man.

A year later the northern tribes invaded across the frontier. Every able-bodied young man took up a bow and went to fight. Near the frontier, nine men out of ten died. Because the son was lame, he did not go, and father and son both survived.

The Huainanzi ends: blessing turns into disaster, and disaster into blessing. Their changes have no end, and their depths cannot be measured. The Daodejing says the same thing in fewer words: misfortune is what fortune leans on; fortune is where misfortune hides.

drumming.title: Zhuangzi Drums on a Basin
drumming.text:
Zhuangzi's wife died. When Huizi came to offer condolences, he found Zhuangzi sitting with his legs sprawled out, beating on a basin and singing.

"She lived with you," said Huizi. "She raised your children and grew old with you. It would be enough not to weep for her. But to drum on a basin and sing: isn't that going too far?"

"No," said Zhuangzi. "When she first died, do you think I did not grieve like anyone else? But then I looked back to her beginning, before she was born. Not only before she was born, but before she had a body. Not only before she had a body, but before she had any breath. In the midst of the jumble of wonder and mystery, a change took place and there was breath. The breath changed and there was a body. The body changed and there was life. Now there has been another change, and she has gone to death. It is like the turning of the four seasons, spring, summer, autumn, winter.

"Now she lies peacefully asleep in the great room of heaven and earth. If I followed her, sobbing and wailing, I would show that I did not understand fate. So I stopped."

The Daodejing says that all things flourish and each returns to its root. Returning to the root is called stillness. Zhuangzi drums because he has seen the root.

turtle.title: The Turtle in the Mud
turtle.text:
Zhuangzi was fishing in the Pu River when two high officials arrived from the King of Chu. They bowed and said, "Our king wishes to trouble you with the care of his whole realm."

Zhuangzi kept holding his fishing pole and did not turn his head.

"I have heard," he said, "that in Chu there is a sacred turtle that has been dead for three thousand years. The king keeps its shell wrapped in cloth and stored in a box in the ancestral temple. Now, tell me: would this turtle rather be dead and have its bones honoured? Or would it rather be alive and dragging its tail in the mud?"

"It would rather be alive," said the officials, "and dragging its tail in the mud."

"Go away," said Zhuangzi. "I'll drag my tail in the mud."

The Daodejing asks: which is dearer, your name or your life? Which is worth more, your life or your goods? The officials offer a place in the temple. Zhuangzi chooses the river, the pole, and the mud.

three-four.title: Three in the Morning
three-four.text:
A keeper of monkeys was handing out chestnuts. "You'll get three in the morning and four in the evening," he told them. The monkeys were furious.

"All right," he said. "You'll get four in the morning and three in the evening." The monkeys were delighted.

Nothing about the chestnuts had changed: seven a day, either way. Yet the monkeys went from rage to joy. The keeper simply went along with what they felt.

Zhuangzi tells this little tale in the middle of a long argument about right and wrong, this and that. People wear out their minds trying to prove that things are one, he says, and do not see that they were the same all along. That is what he calls "three in the morning." The sage, by contrast, harmonises right and wrong and rests in what he calls the Balance of Heaven. He lets both sides walk their road.

The Daodejing's sage "has no fixed heart of his own; he takes the heart of the people as his heart." The monkey keeper is a small, comic version of that sage. He does not win the argument. He feeds the monkeys.

gamecock.title: The Gamecock Like Wood
gamecock.text:
Ji Xingzi was training a fighting cock for the king. After ten days the king asked whether it was ready.

"Not yet. It is still vain and full of fierce pride."

After another ten days the king asked again.

"Not yet. It still reacts to every sound and shadow."

After another ten days the king asked again.

"Not yet. It still glares and swells with spirit."

After another ten days the king asked again.

"Almost. Even when other cocks crow, it shows no change. Look at it from a distance: it seems to be made of wood. Its virtue is complete. Other cocks will not dare to face it. They will turn and run."

The Daodejing says that the best warrior is not warlike, the best fighter is not angry, and the one who best defeats an enemy does not engage him. Ji Xingzi's cock wins without fighting because it has stopped wanting to fight. What frightens the others is not its fury but its stillness.

luliang-swimmer.title: The Swimmer at Lüliang Falls
luliang-swimmer.text:
Confucius was looking at the waterfall at Lüliang. It fell thirty fathoms, and its spray flew forty li. Not even turtles or fish could swim there. Then he saw a man dive into the water. Confucius thought the man was in despair and wanted to die, so he sent his students along the bank to pull him out.

But a few hundred paces downstream the man came out by himself. He walked along the bank with his hair loose, singing.

Confucius caught up with him. "I thought you were a ghost, but now I see you are a man. May I ask: do you have a special way of treading water?"

"No, I have no special way. I began with what was native to me, grew up with what was natural to me, and let things come to completion by fate. I go under with the swirls and come up with the eddies. I follow the way of the water, and I don't do anything of my own. That is how I can tread it."

"What do you mean by 'began with what was native' and the rest?"

"I was born on dry land and I am at home on dry land: that is what is native. I grew up by the water and I am at home in the water: that is nature. I do not know why I do what I do: that is fate."

Nothing in the world is softer or weaker than water, says the Daodejing, yet nothing is better at attacking the hard and strong. The swimmer does not fight that power. He goes with it.

wheelwright.title: Wheelwright Bian and the Duke's Book
wheelwright.text:
Duke Huan was reading a book in his hall. Wheelwright Bian was making a wheel in the yard below. He put down his chisel and mallet, climbed the steps, and asked, "May I ask what words my lord is reading?"

"The words of the sages," said the duke.

"Are the sages still alive?"

"They are long dead."

"Then what my lord is reading is only the dregs of the ancients."

The duke was angry. "How dare a wheelwright comment on what I read! If you can explain yourself, well and good. If not, you will die."

"I look at it from the point of view of my own work," said Bian. "When I make a wheel, if I chisel too gently, the spoke slips and will not hold. If I chisel too hard, it jams and will not go in. Not too gentle, not too hard: I get it in my hand and feel it in my heart. I cannot put it into words, but there is a knack to it. I cannot teach it to my son, and my son cannot learn it from me. So I am seventy years old and still making wheels. The men of old died, and what they could not pass on died with them. So what my lord is reading is only their dregs."

The Daodejing begins: the Way that can be spoken is not the constant Way. Bian says the same from the wheelwright's bench.

woodworker-qing.title: Woodworker Qing Carves a Bell Stand
woodworker-qing.text:
Woodworker Qing carved a stand for bells. When it was finished, everyone who saw it was amazed. It seemed to be the work of spirits. The Marquis of Lu asked him, "What is your secret?"

"I am only a craftsman. What secret could I have? But there is one thing. When I am going to make a bell stand, I never waste my energy. I fast to calm my heart. After three days of fasting, I no longer think of rewards or salary. After five days, I no longer think of praise or blame, skill or clumsiness. After seven days, I forget that I have four limbs and a body. By then the court no longer exists for me. My skill is gathered in one place, and every distraction outside has melted away.

"Then I go into the mountain forest and look at the nature of the trees. When I find one of the perfect shape, I can see the finished bell stand in it. Only then do I put my hand to the work. If I do not find it, I leave it alone. In this way I bring together what is heaven in me with what is heaven in the tree. That is perhaps why people think the work is made by spirits."

The Daodejing speaks of returning to the uncarved block, pu. Qing does carve, but only after he has become uncarved himself, and only along the shape the tree already holds.

peach-blossom.title: The Peach Blossom Spring
peach-blossom.source: Tao Yuanming, Taohua yuan ji (c. 421 CE)
peach-blossom.text:
In the Taiyuan years of the Jin dynasty, a fisherman from Wuling rowed up a stream and lost track of how far he had gone. Suddenly he came upon a grove of peach trees in blossom. For several hundred paces along both banks there were no other trees. Fragrant grass grew fresh and lovely, and petals drifted down everywhere.

At the end of the grove the stream began at a hill. In the hill was a small opening, and light seemed to come through it. He left his boat and went in. At first the passage was so narrow that only one person could pass. After some dozens of steps, it opened out into bright, level land.

There were neat houses, good fields, pretty ponds, mulberry and bamboo. Paths crossed between the fields, and he could hear chickens and dogs from one farm to the next. Men and women worked in the fields. The old people and the children were all at ease and content.

The villagers were astonished to see him. They took him home and killed a chicken for dinner. Their ancestors, they said, had fled the chaos of the Qin dynasty, five centuries before, and had never left. They did not know that there had been a Han dynasty, let alone the Wei and the Jin. When he told them, they sighed.

After some days he left. They asked him not to tell anyone outside. He marked his route carefully and reported to the governor. But when men went to look, they could not find the way again. No one ever has.

bian-he.title: Bian He's Uncut Jade
bian-he.text:
A man of Chu named Bian He found an uncut stone of jade in the Chu mountains. He presented it to King Li. The king had his jade worker look at it, and the jade worker said, "It is only a stone." The king thought Bian He was trying to cheat him, and had his left foot cut off.

When King Li died and King Wu came to the throne, Bian He presented the stone again. Again the jade worker said, "It is only a stone." Again the king thought he was a cheat, and had his right foot cut off.

When King Wu died and King Wen came to the throne, Bian He took the stone in his arms and wept at the foot of the Chu mountains. He wept for three days and three nights, until his tears were gone and blood came instead. The king heard about this and sent someone to ask him why. "Many men in the world have lost their feet. Why do you weep so bitterly?"
