"I do not weep for my feet," said Bian He. "I weep because a precious jade is called a stone, and an honest man is called a cheat."

The king had the jade worker cut and polish the stone, and a great treasure appeared inside it. It was named the Jade of Master He.

The Daodejing says: those who know me are few. So the sage wears coarse cloth and carries jade inside it.

jiufang-gao.title: Jiufang Gao Chooses a Horse
jiufang-gao.text:
Duke Mu of Qin said to Bo Le, the famous judge of horses, "You are growing old. Is there anyone in your family I could send to find horses?"

"A good horse can be known by its form, its bones, and its muscles," said Bo Le. "But a horse that is the best under heaven seems to vanish, to leave no dust and no tracks. My sons have small talent. They can tell a good horse, but not the best. But I have a friend, a man who gathers firewood and sells vegetables, called Jiufang Gao. In horses he is not below me."

The duke sent Jiufang Gao out. Three months later he returned. "I have found one, in Shaqiu."

"What kind of horse?"

"A mare, and yellow."

The duke sent for it. It was a stallion, and black. He was displeased and called Bo Le. "Your friend cannot even tell colour or sex. What can he know about horses?"

Bo Le gave a long sigh. "Has he really come so far? Then he is ten thousand times better than me. What Gao looks at is the working of heaven in the horse. He takes the essence and forgets the coarse outside. He sees what he needs to see and does not see what he does not need to see. In horses like the ones he picks, there is something more precious than horses."

When the horse arrived, it was indeed the best horse under heaven.

The Daodejing says: the great image has no shape. The greatest skill seems clumsy.

sprouts.title: The Man of Song Pulls Up His Sprouts
sprouts.text:
There was a man of the state of Song who worried that his young grain was not growing fast enough. So one day he went into his field and pulled each sprout up a little, to help it grow.

He came home worn out and said to his family, "I am exhausted today. I have been helping the sprouts grow."

His son ran out to the field to look. All the sprouts had withered.

This story comes from Mencius, not from a Daoist book, but Daoist readers have always loved it. Mencius uses it to warn against two mistakes. Some people neglect what they are growing and do not weed it at all. Others are impatient and pull at it. The second mistake, he says, does more harm than the first.

The Daodejing warns about the same impatience. One who stands on tiptoe does not stand firm. One who takes long strides does not walk far. The world is a sacred vessel that cannot be forced: whoever acts on it ruins it, whoever grasps it loses it. A tree you can barely put your arms around grew from a tiny shoot, and it grew at its own pace.

zhuangzi-ox.title: The Sacrificial Ox
zhuangzi-ox.source: Shiji 63 (Biography of Zhuang Zhou); Zhuangzi ch.32
zhuangzi-ox.text:
King Wei of Chu heard that Zhuang Zhou was a man of great ability. He sent messengers with rich gifts to invite him to become chief minister.

Zhuang Zhou laughed and said to the messengers, "A thousand pieces of gold is a great fortune. A minister's rank is a high honour. But have you never seen the ox they offer at the suburban sacrifice? It is fed well for several years. Then it is dressed in embroidered cloth and led into the great temple. At that moment it might wish it were a lonely piglet, but how could it be one then?

"Go away quickly. Do not dirty me. I would rather play and enjoy myself in a muddy ditch than be held in check by a ruler of a state. I will never take office, all my life. I will live as I please."

The Daodejing warns: to fill a hall with gold and jade is to be unable to guard it. To be rich and honoured and proud is to invite disaster. When the work is done, step back: that is the Way of heaven. The ox in silk and the turtle in the box tell the same story. Zhuangzi always chose the mud.
